Failure case: a provider-specific type appearing in the interface signature, or a caller having to branch on provider, fails the spec. Refs: FR-503, US-E2, US-R6, ai-004, ai-005, adp-003, docs/em_fusion_v2.md section 10.

Hosted AI generator, the primary arm. Input: an evidence bundle, a pinned dated model ID, and frozen generation parameters. Output: a validated hypothesis persisted with generator=hosted, model_id, generation_params, and verbatim raw_response. Constraints: uses the provider's native JSON-schema-constrained output so schema conformance is a generation-time guarantee; the model ID is dated, never a moving alias; tests mock the provider and never make a real call. Failure case: a configuration naming a moving alias rather than a dated ID must be rejected at startup, since an alias changing mid-campaign would invalidate the comparison with no visible error. Refs: FR-504, FR-506, FR-507, FR-508, US-R3, US-R4, db-002, ai-001, ai-003.

Local AI generator, the second arm and availability fallback. Input: an evidence bundle and the same frozen generation parameters as ai-004. Output: a validated hypothesis persisted with generator=local, model_id, generation_params, and raw_response. Constraints: schema enforced by a grammar compiled from the same JSON Schema as ai-004, so one schema has two enforcement mechanisms and an identical guarantee; the model server runs on the host and is reached over HTTP as a config value, never as a Compose service. Failure case: the local and hosted arms diverging in accepted schema, or generation parameters differing between arms, fails the spec and would make the comparison meaningless. Refs: FR-505, FR-506, FR-1102, ai-001, ai-003, ai-004, ai-006.

Availability fallback, hosted to local. Input: a generation request while the hosted provider is unreachable, unauthenticated, or rate limited. Output: a hypothesis generated by the local arm, persisted with generator=local, and the fallback event logged. Constraints: no error state reaches the analyst; the fallback is a distinct code path from the correctness fallback in ai-007 and must remain distinct in code and in the write-up; it is deliberately exercised with the network off, not assumed. Failure case: a hosted timeout surfacing as an error in the UI, or falling through to the template generator instead of the local arm, fails the spec. Refs: FR-509, FR-511, NFR-103, NFR-105, AC-07, ai-005, ai-007, ai-010.

Correctness fallback, model arm to template. Input: a model response that fails Pydantic validation or the grounding check in ai-008. Output: a bounded number of retries, then a template-generated hypothesis persisted with generator=template and the fallback reason logged. Constraints: the retry ceiling is explicit with no unbounded recursion, because a retry loop is the realistic route to an unexpected bill; retry rate is logged per arm; this path applies identically to the hosted and local arms. Failure case: unbounded retry on persistently invalid output, or falling back to template without recording that a fallback occurred, fails the spec. Refs: FR-510, FR-511, NFR-103, ai-002, ai-006, ai-008, ai-009.

Automated grounding check. Input: a schema-valid hypothesis and the evidence bundle it was generated from. Output: a per-item grounded or ungrounded determination, a grounding_passed flag on the hypothesis, and a logged catch rate per generator arm. Constraints: this is the load-bearing safeguard, because constrained decoding guarantees shape but says nothing about whether the rule IDs inside the items exist in the bundle; the catch rate is a reportable evaluation result, not merely a safety net. Failure case: a hypothesis citing rule ID RF-NOISE-999, which is absent from the bundle, must be caught and flagged or rejected rather than passing on the basis of well-formed structure. Refs: FR-512, NFR-202, US-R1, AC-06, evb-002, ai-007, eval-005, docs/em_fusion_v2.md section 5.5.

Run-level call budget. Input: a configured maximum number of model calls or maximum spend for a run. Output: the run aborts with a clear reason when the budget is exceeded, and the calls made so far are recorded. Constraints: this is in-code and independent of the provider-console hard cap, which is the backstop; per-call token and cost logging is in place from the very first call, not retrofitted. Failure case: a retry loop exhausting the budget without aborting, or aborting without recording what was already spent, fails the spec. Refs: FR-513, FR-514, ai-007, eval-005.

Generator provenance surfaced in the UI. Input: a hypothesis carrying its generator field. Output: a visible indicator on the hypothesis card and detail view naming the producing generator. Constraints: a hypothesis produced by either fallback path is visibly distinguishable from a primary-arm one; degradation is shown, never hidden. Failure case: a template-fallback hypothesis rendering identically to a hosted-arm one fails the spec, because the analyst would not know the AI layer had degraded. Refs: FR-713, NFR-204, US-A8, ai-006, ai-007, hyp-001, api-004.

Hypothesis Detail header. Input: a hypothesis from GET /api/v1/hypotheses/{id}. Output: title, status, confidence pips, affected area, and time window rendered in the detail header, with a zone map thumbnail and a mini timeline. Constraints: confidence renders through the ui-001 primitive; status is one of New, Under review, Confirmed, Rejected, Inconclusive; the map thumbnail goes through the MapView boundary. Failure case: an unknown hypothesis ID rendering an empty header rather than an explicit not-found state fails the spec. Refs: FR-711, FR-715, ui-001, map-001, api-004, nav-001.

Supporting evidence with traceability markers. Input: a hypothesis supporting_evidence list and its grounding results from ai-008. Output: one row per evidence item showing source, finding, a rule-ID chip, and a grounded marker. Constraints: grounded state is exposed non-visually so tests assert on it rather than on styling; an ungrounded item is displayed and marked as ungrounded, never silently removed. Failure case: hiding an ungrounded evidence item fails the spec, because concealing it removes the analyst's ability to judge the failure. Refs: FR-711, NFR-202, NFR-204, US-A4, ai-008, hyp-001.

Uncertainty and alternative explanations. Input: a hypothesis evidence_against_or_uncertainty and alternative_explanations fields. Output: both sections rendered on Hypothesis Detail, adjacent to supporting evidence rather than behind a disclosure. Constraints: both are always rendered; an empty list renders an explicit none recorded state so absence is visible rather than ambiguous. Failure case: collapsing alternatives behind a hidden accordion, or omitting the section when empty, fails the spec, since the point is to prevent anchoring on one interpretation. Refs: FR-711, NFR-201, US-A5, ai-001, hyp-001.

Decision-support disclaimer. Input: none. Output: the text Decision support only, analyst judgement is final, rendered on Hypothesis Detail. Constraints: always present, not conditional and not dismissible; consistent with the framing in the README and on every screen. Failure case: the disclaimer absent from the rendered detail view, or present only in a tooltip, fails the spec. Refs: FR-712, NFR-303, NFR-304, hyp-001.

Analyst verdict submission. Input: an analyst activating confirm, reject, needs more evidence, or false positive on Hypothesis Detail. Output: a POST to /api/v1/hypotheses/{id}/feedback, a persisted feedback row, an updated hypothesis status, and the new status reflected in the UI. Constraints: exactly four verdicts; the change survives a reload, because a verdict that is not persisted is not human-in-the-loop validation; status transition follows the documented state set. Failure case: a failed POST leaving the UI showing the new status while the database still holds the old one fails the spec. Refs: FR-601, FR-602, US-A6, AC-09, api-005, hyp-001.

Analyst note and verdict validation. Input: a verdict with an optional free-text note. Output: the note persisted alongside the verdict and shown in the hypothesis feedback history. Constraints: the note is optional and never required to submit a verdict; input is validated at the API boundary. Failure case: an unrecognised verdict value must be rejected with 422, must persist no feedback row, and must leave hypothesis status unchanged. Refs: FR-603, FR-604, NFR-402, api-005, fbk-001.

Batch runner. Input: a scenario type, parameter distribution, base seed, and run count between 20 and 30. Output: N completed runs per type, each with recorded parameters, seed, ground truth, and detector output, executed unattended. Constraints: the entire batch is reproducible from the base seed; a single failing run is recorded and skipped rather than aborting the batch. Failure case: a batch that cannot be reproduced from its recorded base seed fails the spec, since every downstream metric would then be unverifiable. Refs: FR-1001, FR-205, US-R2, scn-001, scn-003.

Detection metrics. Input: batch run outputs and their recorded ground truth. Output: precision, recall, F1, false positive rate, false negative rate, and detection latency per scenario type. Constraints: latency is in simulated time per anom-009; normal-baseline runs contribute to the false positive rate, which is why anom-008 must hold; metric definitions are documented alongside the numbers. Failure case: a batch with zero true positives must produce a documented undefined or zero precision rather than dividing by zero. Refs: FR-1002, US-R2, US-R5, AC-10, anom-008, anom-009.

Metrics export. Input: computed metrics from eval-002 and eval-005. Output: CSV and JSON files suitable for direct use in thesis tables and charts, including the run parameters and seeds that produced them. Constraints: exports are self-describing, so a table in the write-up can be traced back to the exact runs behind it. Failure case: an export omitting the seeds and parameters fails the spec, because the numbers would then be unreproducible. Refs: FR-1003, NFR-601, AC-10, eval-001, eval-002.

Anonymised two-arm hypothesis export for blind scoring. Input: a stratified sample of evidence bundles (approximately 5 per anomalous scenario type, ~20 total) processed by the hosted and template generators, one scored generation per arm per bundle. Output: a scoring pack containing the rendered hypothesis pairs in randomised within-bundle order with identical formatting across arms, the arm key written to a separate file, and a blank score sheet per rater carrying the dimensions defined in docs/scoring_rubric.md. Constraints: the arm is not inferable from the exported text, including from formatting artefacts, field ordering, or whitespace; the corpus and the rubric are fixed before the campaign runs, not adjusted after seeing results; the local arm is excluded from scoring and its exclusion is recorded rather than silent. Failure case: an export in which the template arm is identifiable by its phrasing or layout invalidates the blind comparison and fails the spec. Refs: FR-1004, US-R3, ai-002, ai-004, eval-006, docs/scoring_rubric.md, docs/em_fusion_v2.md section 5.9.

Per-arm AI statistics. Input: all hypothesis generations from a campaign, across every generator that ran. Output: grounding catch rate, grounding variance across N generations per bundle, retry rate, actual cost, and wall-time, each broken down by generator arm. Constraints: recorded per arm rather than in aggregate, because the comparison between arms is the result; computed over all N generations, which is a separate and larger population than the one-generation-per-arm corpus that eval-004 exports for human scoring; the local arm is reported here when it ran as a fallback even though it is not blind-scored, since fallback frequency is itself a reliability result; cost and wall-time are write-up material and make the deliberate-spend claim concrete. Failure case: reporting a single pooled grounding catch rate across arms fails the spec, since it hides the very difference being measured. Refs: FR-1005, US-R3, ai-008, ai-009, eval-003, eval-004.

Blind-score ingest and inter-rater agreement. Input: completed score sheets from two independent raters over the eval-004 scoring pack, plus the separately held arm key. Output: per-dimension mean and distribution per arm, the hosted-versus-template difference per dimension, and quadratic-weighted Cohen's kappa computed across the whole double-scored corpus. Constraints: the arm key is joined only after both sheets are ingested, so scores cannot be attributed to an arm during entry; every scored item carries two independent scores, so agreement is reported over the full corpus rather than a subset; the pre-registered adjudication rule is applied to disagreements rather than chosen after inspecting them; a rater who scored only part of the corpus is reported as partial coverage rather than silently averaged. Failure case: computing kappa over items scored by one rater only, or silently substituting a single rater's score where the second is missing, overstates agreement and fails the spec. Refs: FR-1004, FR-1006, US-R3, eval-003, eval-004, docs/scoring_rubric.md.

Docker Compose full stack. Input: docker compose up on a clean machine with Docker installed. Output: frontend, backend, and PostgreSQL with PostGIS running and reachable, with migrations applied and the app usable end to end. Constraints: no cloud account and no external service required; the local model server is a host process referenced by config through host.docker.internal, never a Compose service, because Docker Desktop on macOS does not pass Metal through. Failure case: a Compose file declaring the model server as a service fails the spec, and a first-run start that requires an undocumented manual step fails AC-12. Refs: FR-1101, FR-1102, NFR-105, AC-12, ai-005. Defect found 2026-09-14 by looking at what `make up` reported: the frontend container sits permanently unhealthy while serving correctly. The healthcheck probes http://localhost:8080/ from inside the container; nginx declares `listen 8080;`, which binds IPv4 only; and `localhost` inside that image resolves to ::1 first. Confirmed from inside the container: 127.0.0.1 succeeds, [::1] and localhost are both refused. The check is what is wrong rather than the server -- nginx has no reason to bind IPv6 behind Docker's bridge -- so the probe targets the literal address nginx actually binds. Why it matters beyond tidiness: a service that is always unhealthy can never report *becoming* unhealthy, so the signal was not merely wrong, it was unavailable, and `depends_on` conditions or any later orchestration would inherit that. Added failure cases: a healthcheck naming a host nginx does not bind fails the spec, and a healthcheck naming a port nginx does not listen on fails the spec. Both are asserted structurally against compose.yaml and frontend/nginx.conf together rather than against either alone, because the defect exists only in the relationship between them -- each file is individually correct.

CI pipeline. Input: a pushed commit or opened pull request. Output: backend pytest, frontend vitest and build, lint on both halves, and a basic dependency audit, each reported as a separate check. Constraints: no Trivy, no container scanning, no deployment step in v1; a failing test fails the pipeline rather than warning. Failure case: a commit that breaks a frontend test passing CI, or a lint failure reported only as a warning, fails the spec. Refs: FR-1103, NFR-404, US-E6, AC-12.

Root Makefile as the containerised command surface. Input: a make target run from the repo root. Output: generate runs a scenario batch in a container; demo runs generate then brings the stack up with a build; build builds all images; migrate applies the Alembic revisions against the running database (db-001); db-test-create provisions the disposable test database with the PostGIS extension, idempotently; test runs the backend pytest suite and the frontend vitest suite in containers; up starts the stack; down tears it down with orphans removed. Constraints: every target delegates to docker compose, so the root Makefile needs no host toolchain beyond Docker; backend/Makefile is retained unchanged for local venv work and the two are not merged; this item is blocked on ops-001, since the Compose file must exist first. Amended 2026-08-27: migrate added, and test-backend no longer runs with --no-deps, because db-001's tests need the postgis service healthy and --no-deps starts the backend container alone -- a test target that silently skipped every database test while reporting success would satisfy the letter of this item and defeat its purpose. The containerised run is therefore the authoritative coverage number, since it is the only one with a database. This item enumerates its targets, which makes it the thing that must be amended whenever one is added. Amended 2026-09-04: replay is added, running python -m app.replay in the backend service (adp-007). It deliberately does not use the pipeline service, whose command names a module that does not exist, so make generate is broken today and stays that way until scn-003 -- recorded here because a target that cannot work is this item's own first failure case, and it is being carried knowingly rather than fixed by pointing it somewhere convenient. Amended 2026-08-30 on two counts. First, db-test-create is added and test-backend depends on it: db-001's tests need a test_em_fusion database carrying the PostGIS extension, which was created by hand while db-001 was being built. A manual step nobody has written down is an undocumented first-run requirement, which is what AC-12 and ops-001's own failure case forbid, and it also produces this item's second failure case by a different route -- the tests skip, and the target reports success. Second, this text previously required the native backend/Makefile gate to omit live-database modules when their tests skip. That machinery was specified before db-001 was built and turned out not to be needed: alembic_config resolves paths and reads a committed ini, so it is provable in the unit tier, and app/db/migrations.py reaches 100 per cent natively with no omission at all. The omission set is therefore empty today and the clause has been removed rather than left describing something that does not exist; the rule returns with db-003, where the PostGIS repository genuinely cannot be exercised without a database. Failure case: a target that succeeds while the underlying compose command fails, or a test target that reports success when either suite had failures, fails the spec. A second failure case: migrate reporting success against a database where no revision was applied, or test reporting success while every database test skipped. Refs: FR-1104, US-E7, AC-12, ops-001, ops-002, db-001, adp-007. Amended 2026-09-12: generate is claimed by scn-003. That item creates app.pipeline -- the module the pipeline service has named since this file was written -- so the target stops failing on a missing module and runs a scenario batch, which is what this item's first sentence has always said it does. The carve-out recorded on 2026-09-04, that generate is knowingly broken and stays so until scn-003, is lifted when scn-003 passes and not before. PIPELINE_ARGS carries the scenario type, base seed and run count through to the container, mirroring REPLAY_ARGS on the replay target; the target set is unchanged, so the enumeration above needs no new member. Amended 2026-09-12 again, on landing scn-003: `generate` now runs `python -m app.pipeline` with PIPELINE_ARGS and the carve-out above is lifted. A target is added at the same time -- build-pipeline, which refreshes the pipeline image before a batch runs in it. It exists because the pipeline service builds its own image from ./backend rather than sharing the backend service's, so `build-backend` does not refresh it, and `generate` was the one target with no build prerequisite at all. Found by running it: the cached pipeline image predated SQLAlchemy becoming a dependency and the batch died on an import before reaching any code of its own -- this item's own first failure case, a target that fails while the compose command underneath it is fine. Measured on the first working run: 20 runs of aircraft-coverage-gap over ten simulated minutes each, 52.5 s wall time, about 510,000 rows.

Collapsible navigation rail. Input: the analyst's stored collapse preference and the current route. Output: the rail rendered at one of two widths -- expanded at 280px with text labels, collapsed at 56px with icons only -- plus a control that toggles between them. All three entries and the current-page marker render in both states. Six decisions. First, collapsed is an icon rail rather than a hidden one. Fifty-six pixels keeps all three destinations one click away and keeps the current-page indicator visible; hiding the rail entirely reclaims 56 more pixels and costs both, since nothing then says which screen the analyst is on and every screen change becomes expand-then-choose. DESIGN.md already describes sidebar navigation as slim icons with labels, so the collapsed state is that line with the labels dropped rather than a new idea. The three icons are hand-authored inline SVG path data carried on the route declaration itself, which keeps nav-001's fifth decision intact -- the three screens stay declared once, so a fourth screen cannot be added in a place that has no icon. No icon dependency is added, consistent with TanStack Query and frontend coverage tooling both being deferred rather than taken mid-item. Second, the preference lives in browser storage rather than in the URL, and this does not contradict nav-001. The hash carries the route because the hash answers where you are, and a screen has to be linkable and nameable in a fault report. Rail width answers how one person likes their chrome. In the hash it would give a single screen two addresses and make every shared link impose one analyst's layout on the next reader. localStorage is per-viewer and survives a reload, which is the entire point of a preference. Every read and write is guarded, because storage throws in a private window and can return an absent or corrupt value. Third, expanded is the default -- on a first visit, and whenever the stored value is missing, unreadable or not one of the two expected values. That keeps nav-001's ten tests green without amendment, since they render the app and assert three labelled links, and it means a failed storage read degrades toward the state that shows more information rather than less. Fourth, the toggle is a button rather than a link. nav-001's entries are anchors precisely because they are navigation and carry addresses; the toggle changes no address and goes nowhere, so it is a button carrying aria-expanded and an accessible name stating what it will do. Rendering it as an anchor would be the mirror image of the error nav-001 avoided. Fifth, collapsing hides labels and never entries. FR-701 fixes the rail at three, and a collapsed rail that drops an entry or buries one behind an overflow changes the entry count in a state the analyst can reach. Each collapsed entry keeps its accessible name, so the rail reads identically to assistive technology in both states: the label is visually hidden, not removed. Sixth, this item constrains nav-002 rather than building it. nav-002 specifies the system-health strip in the navigation footer (FR-702) and is unbuilt. A collapsing rail hands it a question it would not otherwise have had: what the strip shows at 56px. The constraint this item places on it is that a collapse must not be the thing that hides system health, which is the same posture op-001 takes for the data-mode badge -- unconditional, not dismissible, not collapsible. That badge lives in the top status bar and is untouched here. Note also that nav-001 cites FR-709 for the health strip where the requirement is FR-702; nav-002 cites it correctly and is the authority. Out of scope, deliberately: auto-collapsing at narrow viewports, which needs a breakpoint decision and belongs to responsive layout rather than here; and the width transition, which is cosmetic and is not asserted. Scope note: DESIGN.md's Panels section states that sidebars have fixed widths, giving 280px for the primary nav. The expanded width is unchanged but fixed stops being true, so one sentence is added there as part of this item rather than leaving the design spec disagreeing with the build. Only the root DESIGN.md is amended; the per-screen copies under frontend/src/assets/Design are generated references. Failure cases. A collapsed rail offering no visible control to expand it, which is a state the analyst cannot leave, fails the spec. Fewer than three entries rendered while collapsed, or an entry reachable only after expanding, fails the spec. The current-page marker rendering only in the expanded state fails the spec. A stored value that is absent, corrupt or unreadable crashing the rail or blanking it, rather than resolving to expanded, fails the spec. Writing the preference into the URL hash fails the spec. Collapsed entries losing their accessible names, so the rail announces three unlabelled links, fails the spec. A toggle rendered as an anchor, or rendered without aria-expanded, fails the spec. Collapsing or expanding changing which screen is rendered fails the spec. Known limit, recorded rather than tested: that a collapsed label is visually hidden while remaining in the accessibility tree is not assertable from this project's test stack. jsdom performs no layout, and the testing convention forbids asserting on CSS classes in favour of analyst-visible behaviour, so the assertable half is the surviving accessible name and the visual half is proven by looking at the running interface. This is the third blind spot recorded on this project, after the frontend coverage gap and the caption defect scn-004 shipped. Refs: FR-701, FR-702, NFR-303, US-A1, nav-001, nav-002, op-001, scn-004, DESIGN.md sections Sidebar Navigation and Panels, docs/em_fusion_v2.md section 5.7.

Frontend data access for scenario control. Input: a poll interval, the backend base URL, and a configuration the analyst submits. Output: the Scenario Control screen reading GET /api/v1/scenario/runs on a timer and posting to POST /api/v1/scenario/start, with the fixture retired from its runs table. Six decisions. First, the fetch goes in the one module that already reaches the network. api-003 made src/lib/api.ts the only module allowed to call fetch, and src/test/transport.test.ts holds it by scrubbing comments and string literals out of every other module's source and scanning what is left. A second module would be a second place the endpoint is known, and changing it would stop being a one-file change. The two scenario calls therefore join the picture's there. Second, the fixture had two halves and only one of them was pretending. scenarioControlMock carries a scenario library -- the five type ids with their names and descriptions -- and a list of runs. The runs were the problem: real seeds from a real batch, indistinguishable from what the database holds, which is what nav-001 had to put a sentence on screen about. The library is not data about the system's state at all: it is the closed set of five types the generator can produce, already parity-checked against the enum, with presentation copy attached, and no endpoint serves it. So the library moves to src/lib/scenarioLibrary.ts and becomes what the app imports, the mock imports it in turn and keeps its shape for the tests that already use it, and App stops importing a mock. Deleting the mock outright would have removed something nothing serves. Third, the table shows nothing until the first answer arrives, and never shows mock rows. This diverges from api-003 deliberately. The picture falls back to the example payload before its first response because a map with nothing on it cannot be developed against, and the degraded badge carries the warning. A runs table is different: an empty table is perfectly legible, and rows lifted from a real batch are not distinguishable from the database's own by anyone reading them. So the fallback here is emptiness rather than fiction, and the screen says which of the two states it is in. Fourth, a 202 has to say something. Start returns at once and the first row can take ten seconds to appear, so a control that changes nothing visible reads as a dead button -- the exact thing scn-004 avoided by disabling controls that were not wired. The acceptance is shown, and what it shows is the base seed the server used: the number an analyst needs in order to reproduce the batch, and one the server may have drawn rather than been given. Fifth, reset and replay stay unwired, for different reasons, and both keep their disabled control with its stated reason rather than acquiring a handler that does something adjacent. Reset has no endpoint at all: api-006 deferred it until there is an in-flight batch worth abandoning. Replay has an endpoint that cannot express it: start takes a configuration and a batch is between 20 and 30 runs (scn-003), so replaying one recorded run is not a request this API can make. Sixth, the poll mounts and unmounts with the screen. nav-001 moved the picture's poll into its own route so that it stops when the analyst is looking at something else; a second five-second poll running against an endpoint nobody is watching would undo that. Failure cases. The runs table rendering fixture rows at any point after this item fails the spec -- that is the whole point of it. A second module calling fetch fails the spec and transport.test.ts. Start reporting success without naming the seed the server used fails the spec, because a batch whose seed the analyst was never shown is a batch nobody can reproduce. A failed poll clearing the runs already on screen fails the spec: the posture is api-003's, which keeps stale truth over fresh nothing. The note on screen still claiming the runs are a fixture, once they come from the database, fails the spec. A screen importing the mock fails the spec, because App.tsx is the seam and no component may know where its data comes from. Scope: two functions in src/lib/api.ts, one hook, the App wiring, the library moved out of the mock, and the note's sentence rewritten. It builds no reset and no replay. Refs: api-003, api-006, scn-003, scn-004, nav-001, FR-806, FR-807, NFR-503.

One batch at a time. Input: POST /api/v1/scenario/start while a batch started earlier is still running. Output: 409 Conflict naming what is already in flight -- its scenario type, its base seed and when it started -- and no second batch, no run rows, no second thread. A start arriving when nothing is running behaves exactly as api-006 describes. Seven decisions. First, why this exists at all, measured rather than supposed. The backend was found hung on 'QueuePool limit of size 5 overflow 10 reached, connection timed out', serving nothing -- not slow, unserviceable, with its container reporting unhealthy -- after several batches had been started from the screen in quick succession. Measured afterwards: one batch is harmless, adding a single connection while /health stays 200 throughout. So the fault is concurrency, not batches. Every start spawns another unbounded daemon thread (api-006's second decision) and every thread borrows the API's one engine (db-003: one Engine per process), so batches compete with request serving for a pool whose ceiling is SQLAlchemy's default fifteen, because nothing sets pool_size or max_overflow. Bounding the count at one removes the observed cause. It does not make the pool safe against arbitrary load, and this item claims only the former. Second, the state lives in the API process and is never written to the database, which looks like the lazy choice and is the correct one for db-007's own reason. A batch cannot outlive the process running it, so a persisted 'running' flag would be a claim no crash could retract: kill the container mid-batch and the row still says a batch is in flight, locking the button until somebody edits the database. db-007 rejected exactly this when it refused a three-valued status column, on the grounds that a process killed outright cannot record its own death. In-memory state has the property that argument wanted: a restart genuinely means nothing is in flight, and the state says so by not existing. Third, this is sound only while the API is one process. Uvicorn is started with no --workers flag in both the Dockerfile and the compose command, so there is exactly one worker today. Adding workers would give each its own guard and silently restore the defect, so a test asserts the single-worker invocation alongside the guard itself -- the guard and the condition it depends on are asserted together, because the guard alone would keep passing while becoming untrue. Fourth, the guard is released in a finally, always. A batch that raises must free it, or one failure disables the button until the container is restarted -- which would convert a recoverable error into an outage, and would be a worse defect than the one this item fixes. This is its sharpest failure case and it is tested by launching a batch that raises and then starting another successfully. Fifth, taking the guard is atomic. A check followed by a set lets two simultaneous requests both observe 'nothing running' and both proceed, which defeats the item entirely while passing any test that starts batches one after another. The guard is taken under a lock, and the test issues two starts concurrently and asserts exactly one 202 and exactly one 409. Sixth, the refusal says what is already running rather than that something is. An analyst who cannot tell which batch is in flight, or how long it has been, cannot tell whether to wait or to investigate -- and the information costs nothing, since the guard is holding it in order to exist. Ground truth is not among it, per api-009. Seventh, the screen surfaces the refusal in its own words. api-010 already shows what was accepted; refusing without telling anybody is the failure this project keeps recording, and a 409 that renders as nothing would look exactly like the defect that prompted this item. The message names the running batch and says the button will work when it finishes. Out of scope, and stated so the item is not mistaken for solving them. It does not cancel a batch -- reset remains deferred, and this item is what makes reset meaningful later by giving it something definite to cancel. It does not report a batch that *failed* after acceptance, which remains the open honesty gap: this item tells the analyst a batch is running, not that one died. It does not give batches their own engine, which stays available and unowned as the complementary fix. It does not set pool_size. Failure cases. Two simultaneous starts both accepted fails the spec. A batch that raises leaving the guard held, so no further batch can start without a restart, fails the spec. A 409 whose body does not name the running batch fails the spec. Persisting the in-flight state to the database, so a restart reports a batch that cannot be running, fails the spec. The screen receiving a 409 and rendering nothing, or rendering it as an indistinguishable generic error, fails the spec. Running the API with more than one worker fails the spec while every other test still passes, which is why the invocation is asserted. Scope: a small guard object with an atomic take-and-release, the route consulting it, the launcher releasing it in a finally, the 409 shape, one sentence of screen copy, and tests including a concurrent one. Refs: api-006, api-010, api-009, db-003, db-007, ops-001, FR-806, NFR-503.
